title: Myths and low-yield habits to drop
introHtml:
These feel productive but give little lasting learning for the time spent. Keep them as short warm-ups at most.

Habit or beliefWhy it falls shortWhat to do instead
Re-reading notes many timesBuilds familiarity, not recallRead once, then test yourself
Highlighting large parts of textPassive; everything looks importantHighlight little, then turn highlights into questions
Learning styles ("I'm a visual learner")Matching teaching to a preferred style has not been shown to improve learningUse whatever format fits the content: diagrams for anatomy or circuits, maps for history and geography, words for arguments, sound for languages and music
Long marathon sessionsAttention and memory drop after long unbroken blocksShorter, spaced blocks with breaks
Rewriting notes neatlyTakes hours and is mostly copyingSummarise from memory instead
Watching videos passivelyFeels like learning, but little sticksPause and recall after each section
Multitasking with phone and messagesEach switch costs focus and timePhone in another room during focus blocks
All-nighters before examsSleep loss hurts memory and reasoningSpread the work; sleep before exams
More resources means more learningSpreads attention thinOne spine, targeted extras
Hours studied as the measure of progressHours don't equal learningMeasure recall, question scores and topics mastered

Almost every habit in this table shares one trap: it produces a feeling of learning (fluency, effort, busyness, coverage) without the thing that actually builds memory, which is pulling information back out of your head. The fix in each case is not to study more, but to swap the habit for something that makes you retrieve, apply or check. None of these habits is useless in small doses; the problem is when they become the main event.

items.title: Re-reading notes many times
items.leadHtml: Re-reading builds familiarity, not recall. Read once, then test yourself.

parts.feels: The second and third time through, the text reads smoothly. That ease (psychologists call it processing fluency) feels exactly like knowing. But it is recognition: the page is in front of you, so of course it looks familiar. The exam will not show you the page. It is like believing you know the way to a friend's house because you recognise it from the passenger seat.
parts.evidence: In the large review by Dunlosky and colleagues (2013), re-reading was rated low utility: it helps a little, mostly right after reading, and much less than self-testing. A survey by Karpicke, Butler and Roediger (2009) found that re-reading was by far the most common strategy students reported, while very few used self-testing as their main one. The most popular habit is one of the least effective.

examples.simple: You read a page about the causes of the French Revolution three times and feel ready. Close the book and list the causes: you get two of five.
examples.nontrivial: A programmer re-reads the documentation for a function until it "makes sense", then cannot write the call without looking. Writing the call from memory once, then checking, would have shown the gap in 30 seconds and fixed it.
examples.html:
• Simple: You read a page about the causes of the French Revolution three times and feel ready. Close the book and list the causes: you get two of five.
  • Non-trivial: A programmer re-reads the documentation for a function until it "makes sense", then cannot write the call without looking. Writing the call from memory once, then checking, would have shown the gap in 30 seconds and fixed it.

parts.instead: Read once carefully, close the source, and answer two or three questions about it from memory. Re-read only the parts you got wrong.
parts.time: Re-reading a paragraph takes ~1 min (~2×). Two recall questions take about the same time (~2×) and do far more for retention.

items.title: Highlighting large parts of text
items.leadHtml: Highlighting is passive, and when half the page is yellow, everything looks important. Highlight little, then turn highlights into questions.

parts.feels: Highlighting gives your hands something to do and leaves visible evidence of work: a page full of colour looks like a page you have studied. But the decision "this matters" is not the same as "I can recall this". Heavy highlighting also postpones the hard choice of what is truly important.
parts.evidence: Dunlosky and colleagues (2013) rated highlighting and underlining low utility. In most studies it did not beat simply reading, and in some it slightly hurt performance on tests that required inference, perhaps because it focuses attention on isolated facts rather than on how they connect.

examples.simple: A biology student highlights 70% of a chapter. Next week, the highlights tell her nothing about what to review because almost everything is marked.
examples.nontrivial: A law student allows herself one highlight per paragraph, only for the rule or the holding. After reading, she turns each highlight into a margin question ("What must be shown for negligence?") and later covers the text and answers them. The highlight becomes the start of retrieval rather than the end of studying.
examples.html:
• Simple: A biology student highlights 70% of a chapter. Next week, the highlights tell her nothing about what to review because almost everything is marked.
  • Non-trivial: A law student allows herself one highlight per paragraph, only for the rule or the holding. After reading, she turns each highlight into a margin question ("What must be shown for negligence?") and later covers the text and answers them. The highlight becomes the start of retrieval rather than the end of studying.

parts.instead: Read a section first, then mark at most one key phrase per paragraph. Convert each mark into a question or a flashcard, and test yourself on those.
parts.time: Highlighting a paragraph takes ~1-1.5 min (~2-3×). Writing one recall question in the margin and answering it later costs about the same and actually builds memory.

items.title: Learning styles ("I'm a visual learner")
items.leadHtml: Matching teaching to a preferred style has not been shown to improve learning. Use whatever format fits the content.

parts.feels: People really do have preferences: some enjoy diagrams, some prefer listening. It feels respectful and intuitive to match the format to the person. The catch is that a preference is not the same as a benefit. You may like podcasts more than reading and still learn the material equally well, or better, from a diagram.
parts.evidence: Pashler and colleagues (2008) set out what a study would need to show to support learning styles: people with style A learn better with method A, and people with style B learn better with method B. Very few studies used that design, and the ones that did mostly failed to find the effect. What does help is matching the format to the content: maps for geography, diagrams for circuits and anatomy, spoken practice for pronunciation. And combining words with pictures (dual coding) helps nearly everyone.

examples.simple: A "visual learner" tries to learn Spanish pronunciation from colourful charts. Listening and repeating aloud would work better for anyone, because pronunciation is sound.
examples.nontrivial: An economics student who calls himself "verbal" avoids graphs and memorises paragraphs about supply and demand. Sketching the curves and shifting them for each scenario would make the logic visible in a way words cannot.
examples.html:
• Simple: A "visual learner" tries to learn Spanish pronunciation from colourful charts. Listening and repeating aloud would work better for anyone, because pronunciation is sound.
  • Non-trivial: An economics student who calls himself "verbal" avoids graphs and memorises paragraphs about supply and demand. Sketching the curves and shifting them for each scenario would make the logic visible in a way words cannot.

parts.instead: Ask "what format does this material naturally take?" rather than "what kind of learner am I?". Then, whatever the format, test yourself on it.

items.title: Long marathon sessions
items.leadHtml: Attention and memory drop after long unbroken blocks. Use shorter, spaced blocks with breaks.

parts.feels: Six hours in the library feels heroic, and it looks good when you tell people. But the last hours of a marathon are usually the least productive: you read the same line three times, and you are tired enough that what you take in is shallow. It also crowds all the practice into one day instead of spreading it out, which wastes the spacing effect.
parts.evidence: On long, monotonous tasks, performance tends to drift down over time (the vigilance decrement). Ariga and Lleras (2011) found that brief, rare switches away from a long task prevented that decline. Separately, decades of spacing research (Cepeda et al., 2006) show that the same total study time, split across several sessions, gives much better long-term memory than one big block.

examples.simple: Instead of one 6-hour Sunday session on chemistry, do three 50-minute blocks with 10-minute breaks, and a 30-minute review on Wednesday.
examples.nontrivial: A music student practising a hard passage for two hours straight starts repeating mistakes as fatigue sets in. Three 20-minute focused sessions across the day, each starting with the passage from memory, lead to cleaner playing by evening.
examples.html:
• Simple: Instead of one 6-hour Sunday session on chemistry, do three 50-minute blocks with 10-minute breaks, and a 30-minute review on Wednesday.
  • Non-trivial: A music student practising a hard passage for two hours straight starts repeating mistakes as fatigue sets in. Three 20-minute focused sessions across the day, each starting with the passage from memory, lead to cleaner playing by evening.

parts.instead: Work in blocks of 25 to 50 minutes with short breaks that actually rest your attention (walk, water, look out of the window, not your phone). Spread a topic across days rather than finishing it in one sitting.

items.title: Rewriting notes neatly
items.leadHtml: Rewriting takes hours and is mostly copying. Summarise from memory instead.

parts.feels: Clean, colour-coded notes are satisfying to make and to look at, and the hours feel well spent. But copying with the source open needs almost no recall: your eyes go from one page to the other, and the information passes through without being pulled out of memory.
parts.evidence: Generating information yourself is remembered better than copying it, and retrieval is one of the strongest ways to generate. Karpicke and Blunt (2011) found that students who practised free recall of a text learned more than students who spent the same time building detailed concept maps with the text in front of them. Even an elaborate, "active" note-making method lost to simply writing down what you remember.

examples.simple: Instead of rewriting a history lecture neatly, close your notes and write the main events and causes from memory on a blank page. Then fill gaps in another colour.
examples.nontrivial: A physics student's "final notes" project would take a weekend. Instead she writes one-page summaries from memory for each chapter, checks them against the textbook, and corrects them in red. The red marks show exactly where to focus, and the pages still become tidy revision sheets.
examples.html:
• Simple: Instead of rewriting a history lecture neatly, close your notes and write the main events and causes from memory on a blank page. Then fill gaps in another colour.
  • Non-trivial: A physics student's "final notes" project would take a weekend. Instead she writes one-page summaries from memory for each chapter, checks them against the textbook, and corrects them in red. The red marks show exactly where to focus, and the pages still become tidy revision sheets.

parts.instead: Write from memory first, then check and correct. Keep notes good enough to test yourself from; tidiness is optional.
parts.time: A neat rewrite of one lecture often takes 1-2 hours. Blank-page recall of the same lecture plus filling gaps takes about 20-30 minutes (around ~4× per paragraph), and it shows you what you actually know.

items.title: Watching videos passively
items.leadHtml: Videos feel like learning, but little sticks. Pause and recall after each section.

parts.feels: A good explainer makes everything look obvious while you watch. The teacher does the thinking, and their fluency becomes your feeling of understanding. It is like watching someone ride a bicycle: easy to follow, no help when you get on.
parts.evidence: Szpunar, Khan and Schacter (2013) split an online lecture into segments. Students who got a short test after each segment mind-wandered about half as much, took more notes and remembered more at the end than students who re-studied the same material between segments. The test, not the extra exposure, made the difference.

examples.simple: Watching a 12-minute video on photosynthesis, pause every 3-4 minutes and say aloud the two main points so far.
examples.nontrivial: A programming student following a tutorial pauses before each step and tries to write the next lines of code herself, then plays the video to compare. It takes longer, but she can build the project alone afterwards, which pure watching rarely achieves.
examples.html:
• Simple: Watching a 12-minute video on photosynthesis, pause every 3-4 minutes and say aloud the two main points so far.
  • Non-trivial: A programming student following a tutorial pauses before each step and tries to write the next lines of code herself, then plays the video to compare. It takes longer, but she can build the project alone afterwards, which pure watching rarely achieves.

parts.instead: Watch with a question in mind. Pause at each section break, recall the key points without looking, then continue. After the video, close it and do a short blank-page recall.
parts.time: One recall pause per section adds about 30 seconds (~1×). Over a 15-minute video, that is 2-3 extra minutes for a large gain.

items.title: Multitasking with phone and messages
items.leadHtml: Each switch costs focus and time. Put the phone in another room during focus blocks.

parts.feels: Answering messages while studying feels efficient: two things done at once. In reality the brain switches back and forth, and each switch has a cost, a few seconds of re-orienting and a thread of thought lost. A 50-minute block with ten "quick checks" holds much less real focus than its length suggests.
parts.evidence: Ophir, Nass and Wagner (2009) found that people who habitually juggle many media streams were worse at ignoring irrelevant information and slower at switching between tasks than light multitaskers. Later studies found smaller and less consistent differences, but the basic finding that switching between tasks costs time and accuracy is well established in attention research.

examples.simple: Reading a novel for literature class with the phone face-up, you check it after every notification and have to re-read paragraphs. With the phone in the next room, the chapter takes 20 minutes instead of 40.
examples.nontrivial: A maths student solving a proof keeps a chat open "only for urgent things". Each glance breaks the chain of steps she is holding in working memory, so she restarts the reasoning repeatedly. Batching messages into the break after each block saves the chain.
examples.html:
• Simple: Reading a novel for literature class with the phone face-up, you check it after every notification and have to re-read paragraphs. With the phone in the next room, the chapter takes 20 minutes instead of 40.
  • Non-trivial: A maths student solving a proof keeps a chat open "only for urgent things". Each glance breaks the chain of steps she is holding in working memory, so she restarts the reasoning repeatedly. Batching messages into the break after each block saves the chain.

parts.instead: Phone out of sight (another room is best), notifications off, and a set time to check messages between blocks. Keep a sheet of paper for "I must remember to..." thoughts instead of acting on them.

items.title: All-nighters before exams
items.leadHtml: Sleep loss hurts memory and reasoning. Spread the work and sleep before exams.

parts.feels: The night before an exam, more hours of studying seem obviously better than sleep. Panic makes the trade feel urgent. But the night you skip is the night your brain would have used to stabilise what you studied, and you walk into the exam slower, less able to reason and with worse recall.
parts.evidence: Sleep plays an active role in consolidating memories: during sleep, newly learned material is replayed and stabilised (Diekelmann & Born, 2010). Sleep loss also reduces attention and working memory, which you need to read questions carefully and solve problems. In a large university course, Okano and colleagues (2019) found that students who slept longer, better and more regularly over the weeks before exams scored higher. Interestingly, the single night before a test mattered less than the sleep pattern over the preceding weeks, so the best protection is regular sleep through the term, not only on the last night.

examples.simple: Instead of reviewing vocabulary until 3 a.m., do a final 30-minute recall session in the evening and sleep 8 hours. The words you reviewed are still there in the morning.
examples.nontrivial: An engineering student with two exams in two days plans backwards: the hardest problem sets go three and four days before, the last evening is only light review of the error log, and bedtime is fixed. She trades two late hours of tired reading for a clear head on problems that need reasoning, not just recall.
examples.html:
• Simple: Instead of reviewing vocabulary until 3 a.m., do a final 30-minute recall session in the evening and sleep 8 hours. The words you reviewed are still there in the morning.
  • Non-trivial: An engineering student with two exams in two days plans backwards: the hardest problem sets go three and four days before, the last evening is only light review of the error log, and bedtime is fixed. She trades two late hours of tired reading for a clear head on problems that need reasoning, not just recall.

parts.instead: Plan so that the last day is review, not new material. Protect 7 to 9 hours of sleep before exams, especially those that need reasoning or problem solving.

items.title: More resources means more learning
items.leadHtml: Extra resources spread attention thin. Pick one spine and add targeted extras.

parts.feels: Buying a new book, bookmarking a channel or downloading another deck gives an instant feeling of progress and safety ("now I have everything"). Each source also explains things slightly differently, which feels like deeper coverage. But every hour spent taking in a new source is an hour not spent retrieving from the one you already have.

items.title: Hours studied as the measure of progress
items.leadHtml: Hours don't equal learning. Measure recall, question scores and topics mastered.

parts.feels: Hours are easy to count and easy to compare with friends. They also reward the feeling of effort, whatever the effort was spent on. But two hours of re-reading and two hours of practice questions are not the same two hours.
parts.evidence: Plant and colleagues (2005) found that, on its own, the number of hours students spent studying did not predict their grades; study time only started to matter once the quality of the study conditions was taken into account. In research on expertise, Ericsson, Krampe and Tesch-Römer (1993) argued that what builds skill is deliberate practice: focused work at the edge of your ability, with clear goals and feedback. Later research suggests practice explains only part of the differences between people, but the core point holds: the kind of hours matters more than the count.

examples.simple: "Studied 3 hours" says little. "Answered 40 questions on cell biology, 70% correct, up from 55% last week" says a lot.
examples.nontrivial: A pianist who logs 4 hours a day mostly plays pieces she already knows. Her teacher has her spend 45 minutes on the four bars she gets wrong, slowly, recording herself. Her practice log shows fewer hours, and her playing improves faster.
examples.html:
• Simple: "Studied 3 hours" says little. "Answered 40 questions on cell biology, 70% correct, up from 55% last week" says a lot.
  • Non-trivial: A pianist who logs 4 hours a day mostly plays pieces she already knows. Her teacher has her spend 45 minutes on the four bars she gets wrong, slowly, recording herself. Her practice log shows fewer hours, and her playing improves faster.

parts.instead: Track outputs, not inputs: recall ratings, question-bank scores per topic, topics moved from "new" to "solid", and gaps found in blank-page recall. Use hours only to check that you are showing up regularly.
